props.title: By the People: The Election of Barack Obama
props.initialSlug: Inside Obama's historic journey to the presidency

sections.content: By the People: The Election of Barack Obama marks a pivotal moment in political documentary filmmaking, following the historic 2008 presidential campaign with unprecedented access. Directors Amy Rice and Alicia Sams secured early permission to follow Obama in 2006, well before his presidential bid was announced, giving them rare intimate footage of his rise. The film sits alongside other groundbreaking campaign documentaries like The War Room (1993), which chronicled Clinton's 1992 campaign, and Primary (1960), Robert Drew's revolutionary direct cinema account of Kennedy vs. Humphrey.

sections.content: What distinguishes By the People (2009) is its capture of grassroots organizing and the ground-level energy that propelled Obama's campaign. The filmmakers deftly balance intimate moments - Obama calling his grandmother on election night, Michelle managing family life - with the massive scale of the campaign operation. This approach influenced later political documentaries like Weiner (2016) and Knock Down the House (2019), which similarly attempt to capture both personal dynamics and larger political movements.

The film's treatment of race and history provides fascinating context when viewed alongside earlier documentaries about Black political pioneers, particularly Eyes on the Prize (1987-1990) and 4 Little Girls (1997). These works collectively chart the arc from civil rights struggles to Obama's achievement, though By the People (2009) maintains focus on the campaign rather than explicitly drawing these connections. sections.content: The technical approach of By the People (2009) reflects the evolution of campaign documentaries from Primary (1960) through The War Room (1993) to the social media era. Where earlier films relied on careful positioning of limited camera crews, Rice and Sams benefited from smaller digital cameras and a campaign comfortable with constant documentation. This shift is even more apparent in later works like Running with Beto (2019) and Mayor Pete (2021), where candidates' own social media content becomes part of the documentary fabric.
